title: Committee backs light rail extension to Cambridge
subtitle: Also: zero carbon standard for Regional buildings, farm sign rules on Regional roads, blue box changes, Elmira truck bypass.
overview: The Sustainability, Infrastructure, and Development Committee recommended extending light rail (ION) from Fairway Station in Kitchener to downtown Cambridge {{vote:m4}}. It also recommended that staff seek full funding from the provincial and federal governments. Council still has to adopt the recommendation. The item drew more than 20 delegations, most in favour, with a few opposed over cost, operating expenses and consultation.

The committee also recommended that new Regional facilities be built to the Zero Carbon Building-Design standard, replacing LEED Silver {{vote:m2}}. It recommended a revised Regional road sign by-law that limits farm accessory signs on Regional roads to signs next to the farm they advertise {{vote:m3}}.

A delegation from Circular Materials explained the blue box transition. A wider list of accepted materials starts January 1, and every-other-week collection with extra boxes follows in March. Under other business, staff discussed the Elmira truck bypass, truck diversion in North Dumfries, ridership trends and a transit ticket pilot for non-profits. The committee also met in closed session on matters including labour negotiations and a proposed land acquisition.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended a full-length light rail extension from Fairway Station to downtown Cambridge, and directed staff to pursue full provincial and federal funding {{vote:m4}}.
The committee recommended adopting the Zero Carbon Building-Design standard for new Regional facilities in place of LEED Silver {{vote:m2}}.
The committee recommended revising By-law 10-030 so farm accessory signs on Regional roads are limited in size and placement and tied to the advertised farm's own property {{vote:m3}}.

debate: Delegates in favour of the extension said light rail would attract housing and business investment, as in Kitchener and Waterloo. They also cited barrier-free accessibility, better links for students, hospital staff and older adults, and the need to avoid transfers on a bus-based option.

Delegates and Cambridge councillors opposed raised concerns about the estimated annual operating cost of $23.8 million, possible cost overruns, and construction disruption. They also raised traffic effects on Hespeler Road, and said a plebiscite or independent cost analysis should come first.

Committee members noted that LRT operating costs are higher than bus rapid transit by about $7.4 million a year. Staff replied that the ION has the highest cost recovery and reliability in the network. One councillor opposed the LRT over the route and cost. Another said affordability should be treated as a separate question during budget talks.

Staff said the townships do not pay for rapid transit. Staff also cited two surveys showing majority support in Cambridge and across the region. Councillors asked about the cost of an elevated guideway, and staff agreed to bring back information.

On blue box changes, councillors asked how residents can return extra boxes and how to reduce confusion over who to call. They also raised that small businesses and places of worship are excluded from the program.
